units.title: Unit 39 — War and peace
learningObjectives: Describe military conflict and escalating violence using precise and responsible collocations.
Distinguish pre-emptive action, counter-attacks, targeted strikes and civilian harm in context.
Discuss temporary ceasefires, vulnerable truces and the longer-term restoration of peace.
Recognise formal conflict-reporting verbs and avoid common unnatural word combinations.

items.example: The two groups remained bitter enemies despite repeated attempts at dialogue.
items.note: Bitter intensifies enemy to describe deep, longstanding hostility.

items.example: The neighbouring forces were engaged in hostilities for several weeks.
items.note: Engaged in hostilities is a formal expression for actively taking part in armed conflict.

items.example: International observers warned that the militia might stockpile weapons near the border.
items.note: Stockpile means build up and store a reserve, often over an extended period.

items.example: The disputed election threatened to create instability across the region.
items.note: Create instability means cause political or social conditions to become less secure.

items.example: The government decided to deploy troops to protect the evacuation route.
items.note: Deploy troops means send military personnel to a location for a particular purpose.

items.example: Diplomats condemned what they described as an unprovoked attack on the village.
items.note: Unprovoked indicates that the attack was not preceded by an apparent provocation; attribution can be disputed.

items.example: Violence erupts when local tensions are allowed to grow unchecked.
items.note: Erupt conveys the sudden outbreak of violence, not necessarily its gradual intensification.

items.example: Violence escalates whenever each side responds to the last incident with force.
items.note: Escalate describes increasing intensity or seriousness after violence has begun.

items.pt: uma série de ataques em pouco tempo
items.example: A spate of attacks prompted authorities to close the border crossing temporarily.
items.note: Spate refers to several incidents happening within a relatively short period.

items.pt: ficar em meio ao fogo cruzado
items.example: Several civilians were caught in the crossfire while trying to leave the neighbourhood.
items.note: People caught in the crossfire may be harmed when opposing sides exchange fire.

items.example: The army was ordered to go on the offensive after its defensive positions were threatened.
items.note: Go on the offensive means shift from defence to active attack.

items.example: The generals debated whether to make a pre-emptive strike before the anticipated assault.
items.note: A pre-emptive strike aims to prevent an expected attack; the justification is often contested.

items.example: Witnesses reported that aircraft had begun to drop bombs near the industrial district.
items.note: Drop bombs is the conventional verb phrase for releasing bombs from an aircraft.

items.example: Officials said the operation had managed to hit an intended target without damaging the nearby school.
items.note: An intended target is the object that an attack was planned to strike.

items.example: Residents challenged the description of the destroyed homes as collateral damage.
items.note: Collateral damage refers to unintended civilian harm or destruction; it can be a euphemism that understates suffering.

items.example: The defenders prepared to launch a counter-attack at daybreak.
items.note: A counter-attack responds to an earlier attack rather than initiating the engagement.

items.example: Commanders described the operation as surgical strikes against selected facilities.
items.note: Surgical strikes implies narrowly targeted attacks; the phrase does not guarantee that civilians are safe.

items.example: The faction attempted to seize power during the political crisis.
items.note: Seize power means take control of a government or authority, often by force.

items.example: Military analysts expect both sides to suffer casualties if the offensive continues.
items.note: Suffer casualties refers to people killed or injured, especially in military reports.

items.example: Humanitarian organisations continued to call for a ceasefire to allow medical aid through.
items.note: Call for a ceasefire means publicly demand or appeal for fighting to stop.

items.example: Analysts disagreed about whether the operation qualified as a pre-emptive strike.
items.note: Pre-emptive describes action taken to avert an attack believed to be imminent.

items.example: The minister argued that a nuclear deterrent reduced the risk of direct aggression.
items.note: A nuclear deterrent is a capability intended to discourage attack through the threat of retaliation.

items.example: The invading army went on to suffer a defeat despite its superior numbers.
items.note: Use suffer a defeat rather than feel a defeat to describe losing a conflict.

items.example: An uneasy truce held for several months without resolving the underlying dispute.
items.note: Uneasy suggests that renewed conflict remains a real possibility.

items.example: Local mediators warned that the fragile peace could disappear if the talks collapsed.
items.note: Fragile describes peace that is vulnerable to disruption; it is not the same as a temporary truce.

items.example: A ceasefire comes into effect tomorrow morning under the signed agreement.
items.note: Come into effect marks the time at which a ceasefire becomes operative.

items.example: The negotiators hope to restore peace by addressing both security and humanitarian concerns.
items.note: Restore peace means re-establish peaceful conditions after a period of conflict.

items.example: An inclusive agreement could bring stability to the disputed provinces.
items.note: Bring stability presents security or predictability as the outcome of an action.

items.example: The agreement requires the transitional government to disband an army formed during the uprising.
items.note: Disband an army means formally break up its organised military structure.

items.example: The neighbouring states agreed to lift a blockade that had restricted food imports.
items.note: Lift a blockade means end the restriction on access or goods, not simply reduce it.

items.example: The commanders agreed to withdraw troops from the demilitarised zone.
items.note: Withdraw troops means remove military personnel from an area; retreat can suggest flight after an attack.

items.example: Representatives signed a ceasefire agreement after lengthy negotiations.
items.note: A ceasefire agreement specifies a halt to fighting; it need not resolve the political dispute.

items.example: Aid agencies warned that escalating violence was forcing families from their homes.
items.note: Escalating is an adjective-participle that emphasises worsening intensity.

items.example: The peacekeeping mission was intended to bring stability to the region.
items.note: This extended phrase specifies where conditions are expected to become more secure.

items.example: Community leaders argued that lasting peace required accountability and rebuilding trust.
items.note: Lasting peace contrasts with a ceasefire or truce that might soon collapse.

items.example: Neutral diplomats offered to broker a ceasefire between the rival groups.
items.note: Broker a ceasefire means help the opposing sides negotiate a halt to fighting.

items.example: Delegates returned to peace talks after a week of renewed clashes.
items.note: Peace talks is the conventional noun combination for negotiations aimed at ending conflict.

units.title: Unit 40 — Friendship
learningObjectives: Describe different degrees and durations of friendship using natural noun and adjective combinations.
Distinguish informal acquaintances, platonic connections and enduring close relationships.
Discuss disagreements, reconciliation and trust using appropriate idiomatic expressions.
Avoid common collocation mistakes when describing making friends or sustaining relationships.

items.example: Mina and Rafael have remained close friends since university.
items.note: Close friends share a strong personal bond, not merely geographical proximity.

items.example: The former classmates became lifelong friends after working together on a community project.
items.note: Lifelong suggests friendship that endures across most or all of a lifetime.

items.example: Two childhood friends unexpectedly met again at the railway station.
items.note: Childhood friends are people who became friends while they were children.

items.pt: um amigo para a vida toda
items.example: After the expedition, Nora felt she had found a friend for life.
items.note: A friend for life implies a bond expected to last indefinitely.

items.example: He relied on a small circle of friends when he moved to a new city.
items.note: Circle refers to a network of friends rather than a single friendship.

items.example: Working in several countries helped Priya develop a wide circle of friends.
items.note: Wide stresses the number or reach of the social network.

items.example: They built a long-term relationship based on mutual respect and shared goals.
items.note: Long-term can describe a lasting romantic relationship or another sustained connection.

items.example: The article emphasised that platonic relationships can offer profound emotional support.
items.note: Platonic relationships are non-romantic and non-sexual personal relationships.

items.example: A dependable social network helped the family settle into the neighbourhood.
items.note: Social network here refers to personal connections, not necessarily an online platform.

items.example: The two musicians remained firm friends despite years of professional competition.
items.note: Firm friends is a conventional phrase for people with a strong enduring friendship.

items.example: Most people at the conference were casual acquaintances rather than close friends.
items.note: A casual acquaintance is someone known only superficially.

items.example: It became easier to make friends after she joined a local sports club.
items.note: The natural verb is make friends, not get friends or find friends.

items.example: The researcher maintained a close relationship with several former colleagues.
items.note: Close describes emotional familiarity or strong ties between people.

items.example: They worked to build a stable relationship after a difficult first year together.
items.note: Stable suggests consistency and relative security over time.

items.example: The neighbours have been on bad terms since the dispute over the shared entrance.
items.note: Be on bad terms with someone means have an unfriendly or strained relationship.

items.example: I hope you do not take the suggestion the wrong way; I meant it constructively.
items.note: Take something the wrong way means misinterpret a comment as offensive or negative.

items.example: The former friends arranged a meeting to heal the rift between them.
items.note: Heal the rift means repair a serious division or disagreement.

items.example: They had a heart-to-heart chat about the misunderstanding after dinner.
items.note: Heart-to-heart describes an honest, private conversation about feelings.

items.example: A relationship breaks down when neither person is willing to communicate.
items.note: Break down can describe the failure of a personal relationship, not just a machine.

items.example: She decided to put some distance between herself and the colleague after the argument.
items.note: Put some distance between people means reduce contact or emotional closeness.

items.pt: ser alvo de críticas ou ataques
items.example: The project leader came under attack for the unpopular decision.
items.note: Come under attack may refer to harsh public criticism as well as physical attack.

items.example: When the volunteers were criticised, colleagues offered to spring to their defence.
items.note: Spring to someone’s defence means respond immediately to support or protect that person.

items.example: Her colleagues offered moral support during a difficult period.
items.note: Moral support means encouragement and emotional backing rather than financial assistance.

items.example: The former partners remained on friendly terms after ending the business arrangement.
items.note: On friendly terms expresses continuing goodwill even without close friendship.

items.example: Volunteer work gave newcomers a chance to forge new relationships.
items.note: Forge suggests intentionally forming strong or lasting connections.

items.example: The new manager worked patiently to win their trust.
items.note: Win someone’s trust means earn confidence through behaviour over time.

items.example: A dishonest adviser may abuse their trust by concealing important information.
items.note: Abuse someone’s trust means exploit confidence that was placed in you.

items.pt: colocar os amigos dela contra ela
items.example: Her rival tried to turn her friends against her by spreading false stories.
items.note: Turn someone against another person means deliberately make them hostile or distrustful.

items.example: The writer discussed her unpublished manuscript only with a close confidant.
items.note: A confidant is someone trusted with private information; close reinforces intimacy.

items.example: She shared the story with a complete stranger during the long journey.
items.note: Complete intensifies stranger, meaning someone entirely unknown.

items.example: Friends can provide moral support without trying to solve every problem.
items.note: Provide moral support focuses on giving reassurance or encouragement.

items.example: They both had to compromise to make a relationship work across different time zones.
items.note: Make a relationship work describes actively maintaining a viable connection.

items.example: A mediator helped the team resolve differences before they became personal.
items.note: Resolve differences means settle disagreements rather than simply ignore them.

items.example: The two researchers managed to remain on good terms after the collaboration ended.
items.note: On good terms is a neutral alternative to the more explicitly warm on friendly terms.

items.example: Regular contact helped the neighbours develop a lasting friendship.
items.note: Lasting emphasises endurance, while lifelong specifically implies an entire lifetime.
